Climate change is expected to have significant effects on the distribution of species around the world. Because many organisms are adapted to specific environmental conditions, even small changes in temperature or precipitation can influence their survival and reproduction. As global temperatures continue to rise, numerous species are shifting their geographic ranges in search of more suitable habitats.

Recent research has documented these shifts in a variety of ecosystems. In mountainous regions, for example, many plant and animal species have gradually moved to higher elevations, where temperatures are cooler. Similarly, marine organisms have been observed migrating toward higher latitudes as ocean temperatures increase. While such movements may help some species adapt to changing conditions, others face substantial challenges.

Species with limited dispersal abilities are particularly vulnerable. Physical barriers, habitat fragmentation, and human activities may prevent them from reaching suitable environments. Furthermore, ecological relationships can be disrupted when species respond differently to climate change. For instance, pollinators and flowering plants may no longer be active at the same time, reducing pollination success.

Scientists use ecological models to predict future distribution patterns and identify species at risk. These predictions can assist conservation efforts by highlighting regions that may serve as important refuges in the future. Understanding how species respond to climate change is therefore essential for protecting biodiversity and maintaining ecosystem function.
